candidateRows: Scientific inquiry strongly confirms theism and disconfirms atheism, so respect for science requires accepting the former and rejecting the latter.
This is Wood's explicit syllogistic thesis and frames the principal case he spends the remainder of his opening attempting to establish.
After introductory remarks, Wood labels theism a hypothesis for debate purposes and presents two premises followed by his science-based conclusion.
Science rests on the assumptions that nature is intelligible, humans can understand it, and acquiring such understanding is worthwhile.
These three prerequisites supply the analytical framework through which Wood later compares the explanatory resources of theism and atheism.
Wood distinguishes ordinary testable hypotheses from a foundational scientific hypothesis and identifies intelligibility, capability, and desirability as its elements.
Christian theological beliefs motivated the pioneers of the scientific revolution and explain why modern science arose in Christian civilization.
The historical account is Wood's principal empirical support for connecting the emergence of scientific practice to distinctively Christian commitments.
Wood contrasts earlier civilizations with early-modern Europe, surveys statements from major scientific pioneers, and infers that Christian ideas motivated their research.
Atheism supplies no adequate basis for expecting an orderly universe, reliable human cognition, or the intrinsic value of scientific knowledge.
The move directly supports Wood's disconfirmation premise by arguing that each necessary presupposition of science is unexpected or indefensible under atheism.
Wood applies his three-part scientific framework to atheism, arguing separately against its grounding of intelligibility, cognitive capability, and desirability of inquiry.
Every successful scientific test confirms presuppositions derived from Christian theism, while scientific discoveries further confirm theism and disconfirm atheism.
This synthesis completes both premises of Wood's announced argument and repeats his ultimate conclusion that science favors theism over atheism.
Wood traces scientific presuppositions to Christian theology, treats every hypothesis test as their confirmation, cites cosmological findings, and states his conclusion.
The historical abundance of mutually incompatible gods makes Yahweh unlikely, and generic evidence for a creator cannot identify the Christian God.
The argument challenges the specificity and probability of Wood's theistic conclusion even if some evidence were granted to support a generic intelligence.
Wood's opening conclusion that scientific considerations establish theism and warrant belief in his Christian God.
Shermer uses religious diversity to argue that most believers already reject nearly every proposed god and asks how creator evidence could select Yahweh.
The Christianity of early scientists is historically unsurprising and irrelevant, while atheism is merely nonbelief rather than a worldview requiring scientific defense.
This reply attacks both Wood's historical evidence and the coherence of treating atheism as a rival hypothesis capable of scientific disconfirmation.
Wood's claims that Christianity explains the scientific revolution and that atheism is a hypothesis disconfirmed by scientific practice.
Shermer argues that nearly everyone in medieval Europe was Christian, distinguishes atheism from humanism, and places the evidential burden on the God hypothesis.
Appeals to God from unexplained complexity are gap arguments that recede as natural mechanisms are discovered and therefore provide an unstable basis for faith.
The move offers Shermer's main methodological rebuttal to inferring supernatural causation from current limits in scientific explanation.
Wood's use of scientific pioneers and scientific intelligibility to infer that unexplained order and discovery support divine agency.
Using Newton's appeal to planetary order, Shermer argues that natural formation theories fill explanatory gaps and make gap-dependent religious commitments retreat.
A creator capable of producing a complex universe would itself demand explanation, generating an infinite regress unless the same stopping privilege is granted to the universe.
This objection targets the explanatory adequacy of God by arguing that divine agency compounds rather than resolves the problem of complex origins.
Wood's broader contention that a rational divine creator explains the universe and the conditions that make scientific inquiry possible.
Shermer argues that a universe-designing being must be highly complex, asks who designed that designer, and questions why the causal chain may stop at God.
The vast preventable suffering of innocent children is incompatible with a God who is simultaneously all-powerful and wholly good.
This is an independently framed argument against the existence of the traditional theistic God and directly engages the debate's evil component.
Shermer states the inconsistent triad of omnipotence, perfect goodness, and evil, then invokes preventable child deaths that cannot be attributed to victims' free choices.
The God hypothesis is explanatorily empty when every favorable outcome confirms it and every unfavorable outcome is insulated from disconfirmation.
This supplies a central methodological objection to theism: an unfalsifiable explanation has no evidential advantage over the absence of the proposed entity.

After presenting innocent suffering as a challenge, Shermer develops the irrefutable-God objection and uses Sagan's undetectable dragon to argue that feelings, prayer anecdotes, and ad hoc qualifications do not establish existence.
Rejecting many proposed gods does not support rejecting every god, because moving from one ultimate creator to none is a substantively different explanatory position.
The move directly contests Shermer's framing that atheists merely reject one additional god and defends the unique explanatory role of a single creator.
Shermer's claim that atheists simply reject one more god than monotheists reject.
Wood answers the one-god-further argument with a podium-builder analogy, maintaining that disagreement over how many builders exist differs categorically from denying that any builder exists.
Atheism is not merely an absence of belief because denying God commits the atheist to locating the world's explanation in some non-theistic alternative.
The argument reallocates explanatory burden to skeptical naturalism by claiming that atheism entails a positive commitment about where explanations must come from.
Shermer's negative definition of atheism as simply lacking belief in any god.

Using vegetarianism as an analogy, Wood argues that a negative label still conveys a positive account of one's alternatives, so atheism invites investigation of the non-theistic source from which its explanations come.
Christian theology was causally important to the scientific revolution because its beliefs about an orderly, knowable world motivated hypotheses that were successfully tested.
This defends a principal theistic case that Christian assumptions explain the emergence and success of scientific inquiry rather than merely accompanying it historically.
Shermer's claim that the religious beliefs of scientific pioneers were irrelevant to their discoveries.

Wood distinguishes his case from an appeal to scientific authority, arguing that pioneers derived beliefs about knowledge and nature from Christian theology, built a testing method around them, and obtained confirmation.
Theistic explanation need not be a God-of-the-gaps inference because Christian thinkers locate evidence for God in established knowledge and the whole intelligible order of nature.
The move answers a central methodological attack by distinguishing explanations grounded in the totality of knowledge from appeals to presently unexplained phenomena.
Shermer's argument that science progressively fills gaps previously occupied by religious causal explanations.

Wood notes that Christian authors themselves criticized gap-based apologetics and invokes Henry Drummond to contend that nature as a whole, especially what is known rather than unknown, is the relevant theistic evidence.
Asking who designed the designer fails because biological design concerns ordered functional parts requiring explanation, whereas God is not alleged to possess that same kind of composition.
This directly defends design reasoning from an infinite-regress objection by claiming that the explanatory property attributed to organisms does not apply to God.
Shermer's objection that a designer invoked for complexity would itself require another designer.

Wood uses DNA's information storage as an example of apparent functional organization, then argues that the relevant arrangement of parts characterizing biological complexity is not a feature attributed to God.
The problem of evil cannot be coherently advanced from atheism unless objective moral law exists and the atheist can justify access to a standard binding even upon God.
This is Wood's principal response to the debate's moral and evil dimension, arguing that the objection presupposes moral resources better grounded by Christianity than atheism.
Shermer's contention that extensive innocent suffering is incompatible with an all-powerful and wholly good God.

Wood steps back from particular theodicies and challenges the moral foundation of the objection itself, claiming that atheists invoke a universal standard they cannot defend while Christian theism can support moral reasoning about evil.
Scientific results are universally discoverable regardless of religious background, while religious beliefs vary geographically and historically, so Christianity is not what validates science.
The move directly counters the historical-theological case for theism by grounding science's authority in public reproducibility rather than the worldview of its pioneers.
Wood's argument that Christian theology grounded the assumptions and successful methods of the scientific revolution.

Shermer argues that physics is the same in India and elsewhere, that discoveries are available to anyone, and that a researcher's religion may motivate a topic without affecting whether measurable results are true.
Apparent biological purpose does not require an intelligent designer because Darwinian natural selection provides a bottom-up mechanism for complex functional organs to arise gradually.
This supplies skeptical naturalism's central alternative explanation for apparent design, directly addressing one of the main empirical motivations offered for a creator.
Wood's appeal to biological organization and DNA as evidence that natural structures require an intelligent designer.

Shermer concedes that wings and eyes look purposeful but attributes their formation to cumulative selection over immense time, adding that calling natural selection God's instrument contributes words rather than a distinct mechanism.
Artifact evidence cannot be generalized to a cosmic maker, and unresolved origins should prompt testable natural inquiry rather than an unsupported leap to an immeasurable supernatural being.

This consolidates the skeptical explanatory method: infer makers where independent evidence exists, tolerate uncertainty, test natural hypotheses, and require evidence before positing the supernatural.
Wood's garage and architect analogy and his claim that cosmic order warrants inference to a divine builder.

Shermer contrasts observable artisans, construction records, and blueprints with the absence of comparable evidence for a universe-maker, then defends admitting ignorance, investigating cosmological hypotheses, and demanding empirical support for anything said to transcend measurement.
Apparently divine acts cannot establish God when sufficiently advanced natural agents could produce the same observable effects.
This challenges whether observations attributed to God can distinguish supernatural agency from advanced technology or measurable natural intervention.
The theistic position that supernatural agency explains otherwise puzzling features and events.
Shermer develops an advanced-intelligence comparison, applies it to miracles and healing, and argues that intervention producing physical effects should be empirically measurable.
The absence of documented regenerated human limbs is strong evidence against claims of reliable divine healing.
The example supplies a concrete proposed test designed to separate divine healing from ordinary recoveries that may happen without intervention.
The theistic appeal to divine action and miracles as manifestations of God's existence.
Shermer contrasts ambiguous recoveries with limb regeneration, demands documentation, and treats persistent nonoccurrence as favoring the absence of divine intervention.
Christian theology materially generated the assumptions that launched science, rather than being an irrelevant trait of early scientists.
The argument supports theism by claiming that modern scientific inquiry depends on specifically Christian commitments about rationality, knowledge, and nature.
Shermer's claim that the Christianity of scientific pioneers was historically incidental to their work.
Wood rejects the political-affiliation analogy and argues that Christian theological commitments generated testable assumptions subsequently adopted across scientific culture.
Unguided natural selection selects for survival rather than truth, so naturalism cannot adequately ground trust in human reasoning about reality.
This is a direct worldview-level argument that theism better explains the reliability of cognition required for science and rational belief.
Shermer's appeal to Darwinian evolution as an adequate natural explanation of complex human life and faculties.
Wood invokes Darwin's own doubt, distinguishes reproductive fitness from truth tracking, and contrasts evolved faculties with minds intended to understand an ordered universe.
A method that classifies every possible divine act as advanced alien technology makes God's existence unknowable by design and is epistemically defective.
The argument attacks the skeptical method at the debate's foundation by alleging that it guarantees a negative result regardless of possible evidence.
Shermer's principle that sufficiently advanced extraterrestrial intelligence would be observationally indistinguishable from God.
Wood argues that miracles, healed amputees, or dramatic manifestations could always be reassigned to aliens, making the method incapable of reaching theological truth.
Scientific success demonstrates that evolved human faculties can increasingly measure, predict, and accurately represent an external reality.
This supplies an empirical answer to the evolutionary reliability objection and preserves naturalism's ability to ground successful scientific reasoning.
Wood's argument that natural selection produces survival-oriented faculties that cannot be trusted about reality.
Shermer acknowledges the philosophical concern but points to spacecraft, measurement, detection, and prediction as evidence that cognition tracks reality with improving accuracy.
God and the supernatural function as vague placeholders at explanatory limits, whereas inquiry should seek mechanisms or discard pseudo-mysteries.
This advances the skeptical explanatory standard that natural mechanisms outperform supernatural labels and directly bears on which worldview explains more.
Wood's claim that being made in God's image grounds human rationality and scientific inquiry.
Shermer questions human godlikeness, characterizes supernatural language as an epistemic stopping point, and contrasts it with provisional scientific terms that invite further causal investigation.
If an apparently paranormal or divine phenomenon were established and causally understood, it would become part of nature and science rather than remain supernatural.
The claim explains why detectable extraordinary entities would be naturalized while an undetectable theistic God contributes no scientific explanation.
Wood's demand for a method capable of identifying God despite alternative advanced-intelligence explanations.
Shermer uses a hypothetical scientific account of mind reading to argue that confirmed anomalies join natural science, then calls the theistic label an unnecessary placeholder.
Demanding evidence for God while admitting that every possible observation could be attributed to aliens makes the skeptical demand methodologically empty.
This sharpens the central methodological dispute by alleging that Shermer requests evidence while excluding in advance anything that could count as evidence.
Shermer's answer that an otherwise unexpected event or advanced intelligence could provide relevant evidence.
Wood observes that the proposed cash deposit and other anomalous events remain alien-explainable, concluding that the method cannot investigate God's existence in any possible world.
Unambiguous limb regeneration would count as unusual evidence, while ordinary prayer outcomes reveal a method that credits God without exposing God to blame.
The reply supplies a concrete discriminating observation and argues that common religious attribution practices are insulated from contrary outcomes.
Wood's assertion that Shermer's methodology excludes every possible observation as evidence for God.
Shermer proposes human limb regrowth as a meaningful case, notes its absence despite prayer, and argues that asymmetric credit and blame prevents theistic claims from yielding answers.
The problem of evil presupposes trustworthy transcendent moral standards and therefore cannot coherently undermine theism from a naturalistic worldview.
This directly answers a principal skeptical objection to God while turning the objection into support for the debate's theistic moral framework.
Shermer's challenge that innocent suffering counts against the existence of God.
After Shermer asks why God permits children to die from disease or starvation, Wood argues that treating this as a problem already assumes a moral law naturalism cannot secure.
Naturalistic accounts reduce moral convictions to biological wiring or social teaching, neither of which establishes that condemned conduct is objectively wrong.
The move supplies the core grounding argument for Wood's claim that objective moral judgments are more intelligible under theism than naturalism.
Shermer's claim that ordinary moral principles remain valid regardless of whether God exists.
Shermer proposes marital fidelity as independently good; Wood accepts the judgment but argues that evolutionary hardwiring and variable social instruction cannot confer objective moral status.
Theism jointly explains objective morality, the universe's mathematical rationality, reliable cognition, and the intrinsic value of knowledge, whereas atheism leaves them unsupported.
This closing consolidates Wood's principal moral, scientific, epistemic, and explanatory arguments into a direct worldview comparison addressing the full motion.
Shermer's naturalistic explanations of morality, scientific knowledge, and rational inquiry throughout the debate.

Wood's closing challenges secular moral grounding, argues that mathematical laws and truth-directed cognition fit theism, and concludes that naturalists retain theistic assumptions without explanatory support.
Secular morality can be grounded in love, promises, reciprocity, social cooperation, and the survival and flourishing of sentient beings without divine commands.
This is Shermer's central constructive account of why binding moral conduct and social cooperation remain rationally defensible without belief in God.
Wood's closing contention that atheists can only assert moral principles without grounding them.
Shermer uses fidelity and promise-keeping to identify interpersonal and civic reasons for morality, then generalizes the standard to the suffering and flourishing of sentient creatures.
Historical moral progress arose through reason, science, and expanding rights despite religious defenses of slavery, torture, racial restrictions, and unequal marriage laws.
The historical argument challenges the claim that religion grounds superior morality by attributing major reforms to empirical reasoning and opposition to inherited religious norms.
Wood's contention that atheists depend upon moral concepts inherited from Christianity.
Shermer surveys changes in slavery, torture, interracial marriage, and same-sex marriage to argue that moral standards improve through investigation and reasoning rather than religious authority.
Human moral dispositions evolved through social cooperation and are culturally adjusted, while genuine internal commitment is favored because strategic imitation is detectable.
This provides Shermer's detailed naturalistic explanation for moral emotions and cooperation, directly addressing the demand for an empirical account of moral principles.
The audience challenge asking what grounds moral principles and whether empirical methods can verify them.
In response to a grounding question, Shermer invokes evolved cooperation, long-term reciprocal benefits, detection of insincerity, cultural modulation, infant studies, and primate behavior.
Evolutionary hardwiring and cultural reinforcement explain the presence of moral feelings but provide no standard for deciding whether those feelings identify what is right.
Wood distinguishes a causal account of moral psychology from normative justification, preserving the principal theistic objection to Shermer's naturalistic ethics.
Shermer's claim that evolved moral emotions and cultural reinforcement ground cooperative morality.
Wood accepts that biology and culture shape moral emotion but uses contrasting reproductive behavior to argue that adaptive necessity cannot establish moral goodness or rightness.
Biblical creation and modern scientific findings can be related through traditions that treat observation and experiment as means of discovering how God ordered nature.
This answers an important compatibility objection linking evolution and cosmology to scripture and supports Wood's broader claim that scientific inquiry fits theism.
The audience challenge that accepting evolution and cosmology conflicts with the biblical creation account.
Wood outlines multiple Christian approaches to apparent conflict and appeals to early scientific thinkers who regarded empirical investigation as the proper way to learn how God structured nature.
Even if morality requires an objective reality beyond humanity, moral truths need not depend on God, and competing religious traditions require human reasoning to identify them.
The move attacks divine moral grounding from both independence and religious-plurality directions, offering a direct skeptical alternative based on moral reasoning.
Wood's repeated argument that objective moral law requires God as its transcendent foundation.
Shermer grants the proposed external moral realm for argument's sake, contends that prohibitions would remain true independently, and notes that people reject many religious rules through reasoning.
Shermer's flourishing and autonomy principles remain normatively undefended under atheism, while creation in God's image supplies humans with a distinctive moral status.
This response crystallizes the worldview comparison by challenging secular moral starting points and presenting divine-image status as the theistic grounding alternative.
Shermer's appeal to individual autonomy and the flourishing of sentient beings as objective moral starting points.
Wood argues that restating autonomy or flourishing does not justify those standards, questions privileging human interests among sentient beings, and grounds special human value in divine creation.
The practical substance of his position is that he does not believe in God and lives accordingly, regardless of whether that is labeled strong or weak atheism.
The answer clarifies the precise skeptical position being defended and separates disputes about labels from the ontological and practical issue of living without belief in God.
The audience challenge that defining atheism as mere lack of belief avoids making an affirmative claim about reality.

An audience member contrasts affirmative atheism with lack-of-belief atheism and asks whether Shermer will assert that God does not exist; Shermer distinguishes several labels before stating his operative position.
Weak atheists may disclaim the stronger naturalistic thesis, but describing their position as merely a lack of belief also reveals that the position itself lacks explanatory content.
It reframes Shermer's distinction as a limitation of weak atheism and preserves Wood's broader contention that skeptical positions fail to supply an adequate worldview explanation.
Shermer's distinction between strong atheism and weak atheism and his claim that the label makes little practical difference.

After Shermer distinguishes varieties of atheism and says he lives without God, Wood acknowledges that weak atheists need not defend strong naturalism but argues that their stated position is correspondingly lacking.
A consoling belief in reunion after death does not answer the problem of suffering unless it is shown true, and competing religious afterlife claims make that evidential burden acute.

The move rejects an afterlife-based response to suffering by shifting from emotional consolation to truth and evidence, while using religious disagreement to challenge confidence in any particular account.
The audience claim that children who die receive everlasting peace and reunion with their families, making death part of a greater good.

An audience member argues that deceased children reunite eternally with their families; Shermer responds that comfort does not establish truth, denies bearing the burden of disproving heaven, and invokes rival religions.
Theism remains coherent in the face of suffering because death need not be the end of a person's story and the worldview contains resources for explaining suffering.
The response supplies a direct theistic answer to the problem of evil by arguing that an afterlife changes the total explanatory context of apparently final earthly harms.
Shermer's objection that afterlife consolation is unverified and cannot be preferred over incompatible religious accounts.

Following Shermer's challenge to the truth of the audience member's afterlife belief, Wood distinguishes proving that belief from showing that theism has coherent explanatory resources concerning suffering and death.
Cosmology does not presently require a divine first cause because quantum events may be uncaused, the universe may have deeper or eternal physical antecedents, and the origin remains unknown.

The response directly supports skeptical naturalism against a cosmological inference to God by offering physical possibilities and treating unresolved origins as grounds for uncertainty rather than theism.
The audience suggestion that the existence and beginning of everything point toward God because the first thing otherwise lacks an origin.

An agnostic audience member asks how the first thing could arise without God; Shermer describes quantum vacuum physics, possibly uncaused events, and eternal-universe possibilities while emphasizing that cosmology is unsettled.
Human success in rationally uncovering a deeply unfamiliar universe is expected if humans reflect a rational creator, but is unexpected on atheistic naturalism and therefore confirms theism.
This is a direct worldview-comparison argument claiming that scientific intelligibility and human rational capacity receive a better antecedent explanation under theism than under naturalism.
Shermer's naturalistic account of quantum cosmology and his conclusion that uncertainty about origins is acceptable without invoking God.

Wood responds to Shermer's discussion of quantum effects and possible universes by asking which worldview would predict creatures capable of discovering such realities, grounding that capacity in divine rationality.
Objective moral inquiry need not rest on absolute or religious ontology because social science can discover real truths about human nature, moral instincts, and institutions that regulate behavior.

The move supplies the skeptical side's positive account of moral knowledge, rejecting the claimed choice between divine absolutes and relativism while grounding moral inquiry in discoverable human facts.
The audience objection that without an independent metaphysical basis for moral truths, Shermer's approach collapses into relativism.

A reader of Shermer's work asks what makes moral truths independently real; Shermer denies that rejecting absolute morality entails relativism and argues that empirical study reveals stable truths about human moral psychology.

Moral emotions and social conditioning cannot adequately bind people who lack those motivations, whereas belief that persons bear God's image supplies an obligation to respect them regardless of feeling.
The response attacks the sufficiency of Shermer's empirical moral psychology through a personal counterexample and presents divine human status as a more universally binding basis for restraint.
Shermer's claim that moral instincts and scientifically studied features of human nature can ground moral principles and civil institutions.

After Shermer grounds morality in human instincts and social science, Wood argues that emotions are unstable and personally absent in his case, while his belief in humanity's divine image constrains his conduct.

Faith is not a reliable truth-finding method, while biological classifications increasingly track real natural groupings despite hybrids because reproductive continuity and cross-cultural convergence provide evidence.

The response defends empirical method against an attempted parity between faith and science, explaining why revisable classifications can remain evidence-responsive discoveries rather than arbitrary constructions.
The audience argument that atheists place faith in flawed scientific taxonomy just as theists place faith in claims about God's presence.

An audience member compares religious faith with confidence in taxonomy and cites elephant hybridization; Shermer rejects feeling as a reliable route to truth and explains how species concepts approximate natural structure.
